prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of optical lattice clocks, whose magic-wavelength trapping brought atomic timekeeping to the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I keep optical lattice clocks first after reading the other ballots. The idea is simple and original: trap neutral atoms at a magic wavelength so the light shift cancels, then interrogate many atoms at once. It was followed by a gain in accuracy of several orders of magnitude, to about 1e-18, which has been checked by comparing clocks in several independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN/Tokyo, SYRTE, PTB, NIST and groups in China). That is the combination I trust most: a clear concept, quantitative agreement between independent experiments, and a result that has been reproduced and built on. It also supports fundamental questions, such as constancy of constants, dark-matter searches and relativistic geodesy, where a clock now senses a height difference of centimetres. The two-name credit (Katori for the concept and first demonstrations, Ye for the performance records and many-body and comb-linked work) is clean, and in this simulation it is the only configuration that fits the three-laureate limit without a painful split of credit. Four members besides me rank it in their top six, and Kroll and Olsson, who judge instruments and measurements, give independent arguments for it.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection is novelty relative to earlier prizes. The 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 prize for controlling single quantum systems (ion clocks) already honoured the foundations of optical metrology, so a sceptic can call lattice clocks a very successful refinement of a recognised field rather than a new discovery. I also think my enthusiasm may be coloured by my own field, since atomic physics is where I judge best and where I may be least critical. Finally, the SI redefinition of the second has not happened yet, and part of the case rests on applications (geodesy, dark matter) that are promising but not yet delivered. Compared with twisted bilayer graphene, which the committee majority ranks first, the discovery content is smaller and the breadth of follow-on science is narrower.

responses.point: Kroll ranks lattice clocks first because magic-wavelength trapping cancels light shifts and thousands of atoms give 1e-18 uncertainty, and he flags overlap with the 2005 and 2012 prizes as the main risk.
responses.response: I agree with the instrument argument and with the credit. On the overlap, I would be more definite than he is: the 2005 prize covered the comb as a ruler and 2012 covered control of a single ion, whereas the lattice clock solves a different problem, namely how to keep the stability benefit of many atoms without perturbing the transition. That is a new physical idea, not a larger version of the old one. Where I qualify his case is on the SI redefinition. I would not cite it as a reason for timing, since a prize should rest on what has been demonstrated, not on a decision by the metrology community that has not been made.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first, arguing that a theoretical magic-angle prediction was followed by decisive, reproducible experiments, and he ranks lattice clocks only sixth as clean but possibly timely or slightly early.
responses.response: I respect that argument and I ranked B033 fourth myself, so we do not disagree on its importance. My reservation is the one that he and Mehlig also list: the pairing mechanism is open, and the transport results depend on twist-angle disorder from device to device. I do not think that undermines the discovery of correlated insulators, but it makes me less sure than I am about clocks that the field has settled which observations are robust and which belong to particular samples. I also disagree that the clocks are possibly early. Intercomparisons between several independent clocks at 1e-18 are exactly the verification we ask for. I would ask him what, in his view, distinguishes the maturity of the two cases.

responses.point: Mehlig ranks the magic-angle graphene first because the Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model is a clean mechanism that experiment tested sharply, and he regards Andrei's role as secondary to the prediction plus the 2018 transport discovery.
responses.response: The prediction followed by experiment is the story I like best in B033, and I accept that as the strongest argument for it. I would put a qualification on his attribution, though. The 2018 discovery was made by the Jarillo-Herrero group, but Andrei's earlier STM work on flat bands in twisted layers is an independent strand, and I would not dismiss it as secondary unless the committee has examined the chronology. As a non-specialist I defer to colleagues in condensed matter, but I would want the attribution in B033 settled before I treat it as a clean theory-plus-experiment trio. My own attribution for B026 has no comparable uncertainty.

responses.point: Pearce ranks the IceCube neutrino discovery first as a new observational window and an instrument achievement, with Halzen as the single credited name, while admitting credit sits uneasily with a collaboration of hundreds.
responses.response: I agree that neutrino astronomy is a genuinely new window and I would not dispute it. I do not defer to that ranking, however, because the whole attribution problem sits in his own caveat: the discovery is the collaboration's, and a one-name prize would honour one leader of an effort in which Karle, Gaisser and Klein, among others, are also decisive. He also accepts that source identification is still at the three to four sigma level and that independent confirmation by a second detector is only beginning, which is the kind of thing I wait for. I would find B024 easier to support after KM3NeT or a comparable result has confirmed the sources.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first and ranks B037 third, noting that circuit QED underlies superconducting processors but may overlap with the 2025 prize, and that a pair cannot honourably receive both Zoller and Cirac recognition.
responses.response: I agree with his own reservation that the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits sits very close to circuit QED, and I think that weighs against B010 this year more than the quality of the physics would suggest. His point about Cirac and Zoller is useful for B037: the trapped-ion entry is not on this shortlist, so the overlap does not affect us here, but it does show that any B037 prize has to choose between the proposals and the experiments.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will see lattice clocks as a distinct discovery or as a refinement of work recognised in 2005 and 2012.

Whether B033 or B037 is the better configuration if the committee prefers a more conceptual discovery; I cannot resolve the credit allocation in B033 (Andrei versus Bistritzer) or the choice of three from five in B037 from my own knowledge.
Priority details for the lattice-clock proposal and the first demonstrations (Katori, Takamoto and others; Lemonde, Ye) are from my own recollection and have not been checked here.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile for B026, B037, B033, B009, B010, B022, B024 or B039. I collaborate closely with Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and the Lund and ETH attosecond groups, but none of them is credited on the shortlist. I have no known ties to Katori or Ye, to the Munich, Harvard or Zurich cold-atom groups, or to the condensed-matter candidates. I am an atomic theorist and share a general field with the lattice-clock community, which I disclose as a possible bias but not as a recusal issue.
